Many people read the Bible, meet in a church, and mark Sunday.
Many people call this faith Christianity. People who follow it are called Christians.
Many Christians believe in one God. People tell the story of Jesus, and many Christians call him the Son of God. Some Christians meet on Saturday, not Sunday. Practices differ from church to church.
The sacred book is the Bible. It holds many smaller books. Many Christians read it at home and in church. It is kept with care. It is not put on the floor.
A common place of worship is a church. Some people say chapel. A very large church may be called a cathedral. Many Christians meet on Sunday. Some meet on another day.

Christmas is a festival for many Christians. People tell the story of the birth of Jesus. Some families celebrate in December. Some celebrate in January. Easter is another great festival. People tell the story that Jesus died and rose again. The date of Easter moves. Families may go to church, share food, and give gifts. Some keep these days quiet.
Many Christians try to love their neighbour. That means helping people, telling the truth, and sharing.

Some Christians fast in a time called Lent. They may eat less, or give something up, before Easter. Some do not. Some churches share bread and a cup in worship. Some do not do this every week. In some churches people dress in a careful way. Practices differ from family to family.
A church, a cross, a Bible, or a candle can stand for this faith. Some Christian pictures show God as a kind wise man with a white beard. Many churches show Jesus instead. Some show neither.
Many Christians say, “Peace be with you.”
A stone church with a pointed spire, a slate roof, and flint walls.
Many people pray facing Mecca and read the Qur'an.
Many people call this faith Islam. People who follow it are called Muslims.

Muslims worship one God. Allah is the Arabic word for God. Many Muslims pray five times a day. To pray, they face Mecca. Mecca is a city. The Kaaba, a cube-shaped building, stands there. Muslims honour the prophet Muhammad.
The sacred book is the Qur'an. Muslims treat it with great care. It stays in a clean place. It is not put on the floor.
A mosque is a Muslim place of worship. Another word is masjid. People take off their shoes. Prayer is calm. Many mosques have a dome and a minaret, a tall tower.

Ramadan is a month when many Muslims fast. They do not eat or drink from dawn to sunset. Before dawn, many families eat. After sunset, they eat again. Young children, and people who are ill, often do not fast. Eid is a festival of joy. Many families pray, share food, and give to people in need. There is more than one Eid. One comes after Ramadan. The dates move, because the Muslim calendar follows the moon.
Islam asks people to be honest and to give help. Many Muslims give a part of what they have to people who need it.

Halal is a food rule. Many Muslims do not eat pork. Many do not drink alcohol. For many families, meat must be prepared in a halal way. Some families are careful about this every day. Practices differ. Never tell a child their food is strange. Some Muslim women and girls wear a hijab, a covering for the hair. Some do not. It is not a costume.
Many Muslims do not make pictures of God or the prophets.
Many Muslims say, “As-salamu alaykum.” It means “peace be upon you.”
The Sultan Ahmed Mosque, with a large dome and tall minarets.
Many people rest on Shabbat and read the Torah.
Many people call this faith Judaism. People who follow it are called Jews.
The Torah is sacred teaching at the heart of Jewish life. It is often written on a scroll. Many Jews also read the Hebrew Bible. The scroll is kept with care. It is not put on the floor.
A synagogue is a Jewish place of worship. Some people say shul. Some say temple. Practices differ from community to community.

Shabbat is a weekly rest. It begins on Friday evening and ends on Saturday evening. Many Jews light candles, share a meal, and stop everyday work. Some families eat a special bread. Hanukkah is a festival of lights in late autumn or winter. It lasts eight nights. Many families light a hanukkiah, a special lamp. People tell a story of a small amount of oil that burned for eight days. Some children play a small spinning game.
Many Jews give tzedakah. That is help for people in need. It is part of doing what is right.

Kosher is a food rule. Many Jews do not eat pork or shellfish. Many do not mix meat and milk. Some families keep kosher. Some do not. Both can be Jewish. Some Jews cover their heads with a kippah. Some do this in the synagogue. Some do this all day. Some do not. A kippah is not a costume.
Many Jews do not make pictures of God. Some story books show Moses. Some families do not.
Many Jews say, “Shalom.” It means peace.
A brick synagogue with a large round window and a carved doorway.
Many people worship at a mandir and at home.
Many people call this faith Hinduism. Some families say Sanatan Dharma.

Hinduism has many ways to worship. Many Hindus worship one God in many forms. You may hear names such as Vishnu, Shiva, Lakshmi, Durga, and Ganesha. Families do not all use the same names. Practices differ.

There is more than one sacred text. The Vedas are ancient teachings. Many families also love the Bhagavad Gita and stories such as the Ramayana. A family may use one of these more than another. A sacred book is kept in a clean place. It is not put on the floor.
A mandir is a Hindu temple. Many Hindus worship at a mandir and at home. Many homes have a shrine. People often leave shoes outside the mandir. A lamp, a bell, and flowers may be part of worship.

Diwali is a festival of lights in autumn. Many Hindus mark it. Many Sikhs and many Jains mark it too. It is not only one religion’s day. Many families light lamps and share sweets. People tell stories. One story many Hindus tell is about Rama and Sita coming home. Some families tell other stories.
Many Hindus try to practise ahimsa, which means not harming. Hosts welcome guests. Helping others is a kind act.

Many Hindus are vegetarian. Some eat meat, and many of those families do not eat beef. Some families do not follow a food rule. Dress at a mandir is often modest. Practices differ from family to family. Never tell a child their food is strange.
A sacred image in a home or a mandir is treated with care. It is not a toy.
Many Hindus say, “Namaste,” with palms together. It is a greeting of respect.
A carved stone mandir with towers and an arched gate.
Many people follow the Buddha’s teaching and practise care.
Many people call this faith Buddhism. People who follow it are called Buddhists.
Many Buddhists follow the teaching of the Buddha. The Buddha was a teacher. Many Buddhists do not pray to a creator. Some traditions also honour other awakened teachers. Practices differ.

A sacred collection of teachings is called the Tripitaka, or the Three Baskets. Some families say sutras. The Buddha taught people to use kind speech, kind acts, and careful thought. Teachings are kept with care. They are not put on the floor.
Many Buddhists meditate or worship in a temple. Some say vihara. Some visit a stupa. Some practise at home. Shoes often come off. The room stays quiet.

Vesak is a festival for many Buddhists. People tell the story of the Buddha’s birth, his awakening, and his death. The date often falls in late spring. Some places use another day. Lamps, flowers, and quiet giving are common.
Compassion is central. Many Buddhists try not to harm living beings. Giving food or help is a kind act.

Many Buddhists are vegetarian. Some are not. Monks and nuns in some traditions wear robes. The robes are a sign of their life, not a costume. Some families fast on certain days. Some do not. Practices differ.
Some Buddhists use a statue of the Buddha as a reminder. It is fully clothed in robes and treated with respect. It is not a toy.
A calm bow, with palms together, is a greeting many Buddhists know.
A large brick stupa under a blue sky.
Many people worship one God and follow the Guru Granth Sahib.
Many people call this faith Sikhism. People who follow it are called Sikhs.
Sikhs worship one God. A short teaching, Ik Onkar, means there is one God. Sikhs honour ten human Gurus. Guru Nanak was the first.

The Guru Granth Sahib is the holy book and the Guru of the Sikhs. It is a book, not a person you draw. In the gurdwara it rests on a raised seat, under a canopy, covered with fine cloths. It is never placed on the floor.
A gurdwara is a Sikh place of worship. People take off their shoes and cover their heads. Many gurdwaras serve langar, a free meal. Everyone may sit together. Many gurdwaras fly an orange flag.

Vaisakhi is a festival for many Sikhs. It comes in April. People tell the story of the Khalsa, a community that promised to live with courage, honesty, and care. Some families also mark a harvest. Around Diwali, many Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas. People tell a story of release and coming home.
Seva means selfless service. Many Sikhs cook, clean, and share. Honest work and sharing are part of the faith.

Many Sikhs wear the Five Ks. They are articles of faith, not a costume. Kesh means uncut hair. Many people cover it with a turban or a smaller cloth. A turban is worn with respect. It is not a dress-up joke. Kangha is a small wooden comb. Kara is a steel bracelet. Kachera is an undergarment chosen for modesty. Kirpan is a small sword. It stands for courage and for protecting others. It is not a toy. Do not touch it. Some Sikhs wear all five. Some do not. Langar is often vegetarian, so more people can eat. Some Sikhs eat meat at home. Practices differ.
The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru for Sikhs today. Some homes keep a picture of Guru Nanak. It is not worshipped. Some families do not use pictures.
Many Sikhs say, “Sat Sri Akal.” It speaks of God’s truth.
The Golden Temple at night, lit gold beside a pool.

Stories say he taught people to love their neighbour. He welcomed people who were left out.

Many Jews tell the story of Moses. The Torah says he led the people out of Egypt.

Many Hindus love Krishna. Stories say he is an avatar of Vishnu. Hinduism has many sacred figures. Krishna is one of them.
He is often shown with blue skin, a yellow cloth, a flute, and a peacock feather.
A picture in a home or a mandir is treated with care. It is not a toy. Some families use a different sacred image.
A drawing of the Buddha seated in orange robes, with a calm face.
The Buddha was a teacher. His name was Siddhartha Gautama.
He taught a calm way to understand suffering, and to be kind.
Many Buddhists use a picture or a statue as a reminder. The figure wears robes. It is not a toy.
A drawing of Guru Nanak seated, with a beard, an orange turban, and prayer beads.
Guru Nanak was the first Sikh Guru. He taught that there is one God, and that people are equal.
Some homes keep a picture of him. The picture is not worshipped. Some families do not use a picture.
Sikhs today treat the Guru Granth Sahib as their Guru. That book is kept with great care. Many Sikhs do not draw God.
People tell the story that Jesus died and rose again. Many families go to church. Some share a meal. Some keep the day quiet.
People tell the story of the Khalsa, a community that promised courage, honesty, and care. Some families also mark a harvest. Many people go to a gurdwara and share langar.
Late spring. The date can differ.
People tell the story of the Buddha’s birth, his awakening, and his death. Many people offer lamps or flowers. Some places use another day. The day stays calm.
The dates move through the year.

In Ramadan, many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. Young children, and people who are ill, often do not fast. Eid comes after Ramadan. It is a festival of prayer, food, and giving. There is more than one Eid. The Muslim calendar follows the moon, so the dates move.

Diwali is a festival of lights. It is not only one religion’s day. Many Hindus light lamps and share sweets. People tell stories, and families do not all tell the same one. Many Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas around this time. Many Jains remember the teacher Mahavira.
Late autumn or winter. The date moves.

Hanukkah lasts eight nights. Many families light a hanukkiah. People tell a story of a small amount of oil that burned for eight days. Shabbat is different. It is not once a year. Many Jews rest every week, from Friday evening to Saturday evening.

People tell the story of the birth of Jesus. Many families go to church, share food, and give gifts. Some celebrate in December. Some celebrate in January. Some families with no religion still share a meal on this public day. Some do not.

People may be praying. Sit still. If you do not pray, that is all right. Do not copy a prayer as a joke. Do not talk over it.
Follow the host. Do not run. Do not climb on furniture. Do not sit on a holy book.
Shoes off when that is the custom
Many mosques, gurdwaras, mandirs, and temples ask you to remove your shoes. Many churches do not. If you are not sure, ask.
Cover your head if you are asked
In a gurdwara, people cover their heads. Some synagogues, churches, and mosques offer a covering too. If someone offers you one, wear it while you are inside. It is not a costume.
Some places say no photos. Some say no photos during prayer. Wait for a yes. Do not take a photo of a person who looks away.
Leave holy things in their place
Do not touch a holy book, a statue, or a scroll unless a host shows you how. Do not put a sacred book on the floor. Do not touch a kirpan.
If food is offered and you can eat it, you may say thank you. If you cannot eat it, say “No thank you.” Do not call the food strange.
Thank the host. Walk slowly. A good guest makes the next guest welcome too.

People in these faiths live all over the world. Each stop is one kind of place of worship. The stops are the same size.
Many families pray or worship. Some do this in a building. Some do this at home. Some sit in silence. Some sing. Some do not pray at all.
Many Christians read the Bible and mark Sunday. Some mark Saturday. Prayer in church is often calm.
Many Muslims pray facing Mecca. Prayer in a mosque is calm. Shoes come off.
Many Jews rest on Shabbat and may pray in a synagogue.
Many Hindus worship at a mandir and at home.
Many Buddhists follow the Buddha’s teaching. Many do not pray to a creator. Some meditate in a temple or at home.
Sikhs worship one God. Many pray and sing in a gurdwara. The Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat.
Christmas and Easter are Christian festivals. People tell the story of Jesus at both. Some families celebrate Christmas in December. Some celebrate it in January. The date of Easter moves.
Ramadan and Eid are Muslim festivals. In Ramadan, many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset. Young children often do not fast. Eid is a joyful day of prayer, food, and giving. The dates move.
Shabbat and Hanukkah are Jewish festivals. Shabbat is every week, from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Many Jews rest. Hanukkah is a festival of lights for eight nights.
Diwali is a festival many Hindus, Sikhs, and Jains mark. It is not only one religion’s day. Many families light lamps. People tell different stories.
Vesak is a festival for many Buddhists. People tell the story of the Buddha’s birth, awakening, and death. The date can differ.
Vaisakhi is a festival for many Sikhs. It comes in April. People tell the story of the Khalsa.
Some families with no religion still share a public holiday. Some do not. Practices differ from family to family.
Halal and kosher are food rules. Halal is a rule many Muslims follow. Many do not eat pork. Kosher is a rule many Jews follow. Many do not eat pork or shellfish, and many do not mix meat and milk.
Some families follow these rules every day. Some do not. Both can belong to the faith.
Many Hindus are vegetarian. Some are not. Many Buddhists are vegetarian. Some are not. Langar, the shared meal at many gurdwaras, is often vegetarian so more people can eat.
Some families fast. Some do not. A fast can mean no food and no drink for part of a day. It can mean eating less. Children are often not asked to fast.
Never tell a child their food is strange. If you cannot eat something, say “No thank you.”
Many faiths ask people to be kind. The words differ. The care can look alike.

Many Christians try to love their neighbour. Many Muslims try to be honest and to give help. Many Jews give tzedakah. Many Hindus and many Jains try not to harm. Many Buddhists practise compassion. Many Sikhs offer seva, which is service, and share langar.
Many Bahá’ís work for peace. Many people with no religion still try to be fair.
A kind class leaves room for all of these, and for families who do not follow a religion.

Bahá’í, Jainism, and families with no religion
The Khanda is a Sikh symbol.
Many people call this faith the Bahá’í Faith. Bahá’ís worship one God. They follow the teachings of Bahá’u’lláh.
He taught that all people belong to one human family. Sacred writings guide prayer and daily life. Many Bahá’í families do not use pictures of Bahá’u’lláh.
Many Bahá’ís meet in homes. A Bahá’í House of Worship is open to everyone. Many have nine sides and a quiet garden.
Many adults fast for nineteen days in the year. Children are not asked to fast. A kind act is to tell the truth and to work for peace. Practices differ from family to family.
Many people call this faith Jainism. A central teaching is ahimsa. That means non-violence toward living beings.
Many Jains follow the path taught by Mahavira and other teachers called Tirthankaras.
A place of worship may be called a derasar or a temple. Many Jains are vegetarian. Some also avoid honey or root vegetables. Some do not. Practices differ.
Many Jains mark Diwali. People tell the story of Mahavira at that time. A kind act is to walk carefully, and to speak in a way that does not hurt.

Some people do not follow a religion. Some say they are atheist, which means they do not believe in a god. Some say they are agnostic, which means they do not claim to know. Some say humanist, which means they care about human kindness and fairness. Some simply say none.
These families are a real part of the world. They may still have rest days, birthdays, and meals together. Some mark a public holiday. Some do not.
There is no one sacred book and no one place of worship. Some people love a library, a park, or home. There is no shared food rule. Never call their food strange.
They can be kind. They are not a mistake. A class includes them with the same respect.
